q: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'a@b.com'` has no index on email. What does Postgres do?
options: Reads the whole table, row by row (a Seq Scan), even though you want one row
Jumps straight to the row, because email is unique
Builds a temporary index first, then uses it
Refuses to run the query
why: Without an index, the work grows with the table, even when you want 1 row.

q: Which of these can a B-tree index help with?
options: Only `=`
`=`, `<`, `>`, BETWEEN and ORDER BY
Only text columns
Only the primary key
why: A B-tree keeps values sorted, so it helps with order and ranges, not only equality.

q: What is the cost of adding an index?
options: Reads get slower
The table can no longer be updated
Every INSERT gets slower, and the index takes disk space
Nothing, indexes are free
why: Index only what your real slow queries use.

q: You made an index, but EXPLAIN shows a Seq Scan, and the filter matches 60% of the table. What is the right conclusion?
options: Postgres has a bug. Run REINDEX
The index is broken and must be dropped
You must force the index with a hint
The Seq Scan is the correct, faster choice here. Reading the table is cheaper than jumping back and forth
why: An index helps when few rows match. When most rows match, reading the table is cheaper. Run EXPLAIN and check.

q: Which column gets an index automatically in Postgres?
options: The primary key, and UNIQUE columns
Every foreign key column
Every column in a WHERE
Every column named id_something
why: A foreign key does NOT get an index. Add that index yourself.
